summary: Shows that off-the-shelf text+image coding agents (Codex with GPT-5.4, Claude Code with Opus/Sonnet 4.6, plus MiniMax/Kimi) in a sandbox with ffmpeg/ASR/OCR tooling can match or beat native omni-modal models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.5-Omni, etc.) on four audio/video QA benchmarks by writing code to extract transcripts/frames instead of ingesting raw media. Adds a 200-trajectory failure taxonomy, a skill-injection study (human-written, calibration-set self-iteration, log-driven self-distilled skills), an SFT+GSPO training recipe (Code-X, 6,035-example OmniCoding dataset) for Qwen 9B/27B, and a 50-task processing benchmark (TerminalBench-O).

claims.claim: Codex GPT-5.4 xhigh reaches 75.0% on OmniGAIA, beating the best native omni model Gemini 3.1 Pro (66.1).
claims.evidence: Table 1 and §2.1 text (line 341) match the abstract/intro. Single pass@1 run, no variance; web search allowed during evaluation with manual trajectory inspection for leakage (§2 Environments). Native models lead on SocialOmni Level-1 and LVOmniBench overall, so 'competitive' is benchmark-dependent; SocialOmni/LVOmniBench use only first 100 examples per level.

claims.claim: Coding agents use far fewer input tokens than native omni models by selectively extracting evidence.
claims.evidence: Figure 3 average input tokens vs accuracy; trajectory analysis. Dollar cost/latency of long agent runs not reported.

claims.claim: Skill injection substantially improves performance (61.4% -> 76.7% on OmniGAIA); trace-distilled skills beat human-written and calibration-set skills.
claims.evidence: Figure 7, GPT-5.4 high only, single run. Baseline is GPT-5.4 high (61.4), while xhigh without skills already scores 75.0, so the gain is partly substituting for reasoning effort. Distillation prompts (App. H.2) instruct the skill writer to avoid hints for 'the exact benchmark subset', implying skills were mined from runs on the same benchmark: held-out separation is not clearly established.

claims.claim: Code-X 27B reaches 43.3% on OmniGAIA and 60.0% on LVOmniBench, SOTA among open-source models.
claims.evidence: Table 4 (§3.3) contains 43.3 and 60.0 for the 27B RL model; baselines are the same base models without training and an SFT-only warm-up; pass@1, no seeds.

claims.claim: Even GPT-5.5 Codex reaches only 24% on TerminalBench-O.
claims.evidence: Table 5; 50 tasks graded on 4-8 weighted dimensions partly by an LLM-based judge (Fig. 9); LLM process-judge agreement studied on 200 trajectories (Table 8) but TerminalBench-O judge itself not validated against humans in main text.

patterns.note: Code-as-action/CLI-first tooling in a sandbox beats predefined multimodal scaffolds (OmniAgent, Agent-Omni) and many native models on tool-oriented benchmarks.
Isolated Ubuntu workspace with staged files and free package install is the enabling harness; no security evaluation of the sandbox.
Inference-time Skills packages improve accuracy (Fig. 7), with caveats on held-out separation and single run.
Log-driven self-distilled skills outperform calibration-set self-iteration and human skills, but likely mined on the evaluation benchmark.
SFT + GSPO with process-aware verifiable reward improves Qwen 9B/27B over untrained baselines.
Introduces TerminalBench-O; authors' benchmark, authors' recipe evaluated on it.
LLM-based judges used for TerminalBench-O grading and process-level trajectory evaluation (Table 8).

[retag 2026-10-07] Agent-Omni runs a fixed multi-agent graph (modality summarization -> master reasoning -> modality execution -> master decision, max 2 rounds; App. H.3.1). With the same GPT-5.4-high backbone it trails the open Codex coding loop on all four benchmarks (Table 1): OmniGAIA avg 41.1 vs 61.4, SocialOmni L1 37.0 vs 72.0, LVOmniBench avg 36.0 vs 58.0, VideoZeroBench 5.0 vs 27.2. It also trails the iterative OmniAgent controller on 3 of 4 (OmniGAIA 41.1 vs 66.4). Confounded by tool/sandbox access and round budget; single pass@1 run; multimodal QA, not code.

methodology.sample: Four benchmarks (OmniGAIA 360 QA; SocialOmni and LVOmniBench first 100 per level; VideoZeroBench), 200 sampled trajectories for failure taxonomy, TerminalBench-O 50 tasks.
methodology.baselines: Native omni models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen 3.5-Omni, MiMo-V2-Omni) and modular omni agents (OmniAgent, Agent-Omni with GPT-5.4 high) — current and strong; plus text-only ablation.
methodology.models: GPT-5.4 low/medium/high/xhigh, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, MiniMax M2.7, Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V4; Qwen3.5-9B/Qwen3.6-27B trained. Opus 4.6/4.7 results incomplete (Limitations).
methodology.variance: pass@1, single run; no seeds or CIs on main tables.
methodology.ablations: Reasoning effort sweep, text-only vs vision ablation, skill settings, SFT vs RL.
methodology.contamination_controls: Manual trajectory inspection for answer leakage/evaluator hacking with web access enabled; skill-writer prompts forbid copying question content; no formal held-out split for skills described.
methodology.languages: Agents write Python/shell scripts; tasks are multimodal QA/processing, not software engineering.

standards.artifacts: Code 'will be available' at github.com/Dongping-Chen/OmniCoding; prompts in App. H; dataset/benchmark described as to be open-sourced.

biases.detail: All main results are single pass@1 runs of stochastic agent harnesses.
Web search allowed during evaluation of public benchmarks; skills likely distilled from runs on the same benchmark.
TerminalBench-O and Code-X are both by the authors; the benchmark's scores partly come from an LLM judge they configured.
TerminalBench-O grading uses an LLM judge without reported human agreement in the main text.
Token counts reported but not dollar cost or wall-clock for xhigh-effort agent runs.
Text-only ablation shows many benchmark items are solvable via OCR/text, so 'omni-modal competence' is partly a benchmark artifact (acknowledged §2.1).

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Evaluates OpenAI Codex/GPT and Anthropic Claude Code as third parties; authors' own Code-X and TerminalBench-O.
coi.detail: No vendor affiliation; mild self-evaluation of own benchmark and recipe.

verdict_reason: Strong, current baselines and many frontier models make the main 'coding agents are competitive' result credible on tool-oriented benchmarks, but everything is single-run pass@1 with web access, the skill-injection gain likely lacks held-out separation and is on one model, and the new benchmark is LLM-judged by the authors. Domain is multimodal QA, not software engineering.
applicability: Indirectly useful for the domain ingestion: if ingestion includes lecture video/audio or scanned documents, a sandboxed coding agent orchestrating ffmpeg/ASR/OCR into structured artifacts is a viable alternative to a native multimodal model, and cheaper in tokens. For harness decisions it supports a CLI-first, sandboxed tool interface that works identically across hosts (the study ran both Codex and Claude Code harnesses unmodified) and on-demand Skills, but the skill numbers should not be trusted without a held-out evaluation in the team's own repos. Nothing here addresses Java, multi-repo coordination, or spec-driven development; TerminalBench-O's 'spec-compliant outputs' are format checks, not specs.
